text: This horror demo promises no jumpscares. Its build quietly makes the same kind of promise about everything else.
There is exactly one non-engine assembly in it. One.
Let's do the game first.
The No Jumpscare Show. In its world the paranormal is ordinary, and jumpscares are a lazy cliche everybody is tired of.
So a girl called Illy signs up for a haunted house that advertises the opposite. Real psychological horror, no cheap shots.
Survive the night without getting scared and you win ten thousand dollars.
It's black and white. All of it. Not drained of colour afterwards, built that way, with checkerboard floors and paper faces.
And the monsters have names, and they talk to you. Thingy. Skelly Billy. Manicus, who says hello and thanks you for coming to the show.
That's the joke and the threat in one move. Nothing leaps out. Things walk up and start a conversation.
It went up yesterday. English only, four reviews, and a full game with no date on it.
Which leaves the build.
Three hundred and thirty-nine megabytes. Two hundred and sixty-two files.
Unity, on the Mono backend. Mono matters here, because it means the assembly list is readable instead of compiled away.
That list is where every one of these episodes has found its story. Who they bought from. What they forgot to take out.
So here is this one, in full.
Assembly-CSharp. Their own code, compiled. And then nothing.
No DOTween. No Odin. No Steamworks wrapper, no asset-store shaders, no text animator, no save system, no pathfinding library.
A haunted-house demo that went up the same day carries more than forty of those.
There's no StreamingAssets folder either. No Plugins folder.
And no folder called BackUpThisFolder_ButDontShipItWithYourGame. Unity writes that name for you, and three demos I've opened this month shipped it anyway.
The hundred and eight DLLs in here are all Unity's own.
So if three hundred megabytes didn't go into packages, where did it go?
Into the rooms. level10 on its own is seventy-two megabytes. One scene, twenty-one percent of the game.
Ninety-eight megabytes of resource files and sixty-two of resS beside it. Audio and textures, sitting exactly where Unity leaves them when nobody has built a pipeline.
It is the plainest build I have opened on this channel.
Reception is four reviews and one day. There's nothing to read there yet.
So here's the honest read. This is what it looks like when a small team writes the thing and doesn't go shopping.
That is not automatically better, and I want to be clear about it. Bought packages are how small teams ship at all. I've said exactly that about six demos in a row.
But after fifteen builds where the story was what somebody left in, a list with nothing on it is worth stopping on.
Here's the whole teardown on one card.
Unity on Mono, three hundred and thirty-nine megabytes, two hundred and sixty-two files, and one assembly that isn't the engine's — which is theirs.
Worth a dip. It's free, it's genuinely strange, and a monster that introduces itself politely turns out to be worse than one that jumps.
If you ship in Unity, open your own Managed folder and count what's in it. There's no prize for a short list. But there is a lot of information in yours.
That's my read from the outside. If you worked on this and I got something wrong, say so and I'll pin the correction. Next time, another demo, another file list. This is Demo Dip.
